title: Meeting Design - Meeting OS
subtitle: Make every meeting earn its time or cancel it
useWhen: Your team spends too much time in meetings that end without clear decisions or actions. People leave unclear on what was agreed, who will do what, or why the meeting needed to happen at all.
howToUse: Drawing from Patrick Lencioni's work on organisational health and broader meeting efficiency research, the Meeting OS is a set of design principles for every recurring and ad hoc meeting: define the meeting type (decision, discussion, update, or brainstorm), set the agenda 24 hours in advance, start with the most important item first, assign one facilitator, end with explicit decisions and owners recorded, and send a summary within an hour. AI can design a complete meeting operating system for any team structure.
steps: Define the type of every standing meeting most teams mix types and get the worst of each.
Put the hardest agenda item first energy and attention decline through a meeting, not increase.
End every meeting with the read-out: what was decided, who owns it, by when.

Audit all standing meetings quarterly, cancel any that have become status updates disguised as collaboration. Sending a summary within an hour doesn't mean the meeting worked. If the read-out says "we discussed X" instead of "we decided X, owner Y, by Z," the meeting still didn't earn its time. A Read-Out Isn't a Decision
origin: Patrick Lencioni, Death by Meeting, 2004 · Meeting efficiency research
promptBody:
Act as an organisational design consultant specialising in meeting efficiency.
My team                : [SIZE, ROLES, WORKING STYLE  REMOTE / IN-PERSON / HYBRID]
Current meetings: [LIST YOUR STANDING MEETINGS AND THEIR FREQUENCY]

Design a complete Meeting OS for my team:

STANDING MEETINGS: For each existing meeting

                                   reformatted?

proTip:
The most productive meeting reform any team can make is adding a mandatory read-
out at the end of every meeting: 'What did we decide? Who owns each action? By
when?' This 3-minute habit prevents the most common meeting failure,  leaving with
different understandings of what was agreed.
